title: Indian American Philanthropists in Dallas Reaffirm Local Giving Amid Divisive Rhetoric
excerpt: Indiaspora and the India Philanthropy Alliance used their Dallas summit to stress seva at home — neighbourhoods, nonprofits and universities — alongside giving to India.
body:
• Indiaspora and the India Philanthropy Alliance used their annual Philanthropy Summit in Dallas to reaffirm Indian American giving to local neighbourhoods, nonprofits and universities in the United States.
  • The Oct. 14 statement, issued via GlobeNewswire, directly answers recent racially charged rhetoric directed at Indian Americans, framing local giving as relationship- and trust-building.
  • Summit priorities included stronger nonprofit staffing and training, engaging young professionals, and more support for preventive health.
  • For readers: the companion Dallas summit on Sept. 28-29 drew more than 160 leaders, and the next India Giving Day is scheduled for March 12, 2027.

Indian American philanthropists have publicly reaffirmed their commitment to the American communities where they live, in a statement issued as Indiaspora and the India Philanthropy Alliance (IPA) marked their annual Philanthropy Summit in Dallas.

The statement, released Oct. 14 via GlobeNewswire and reported by The Manila Times, places local giving at the centre of the community's story. It describes philanthropy as one of Indiaspora's core pillars and invokes seva, or selfless service, as a guiding value. Crucially, it does not frame giving to the United States and giving to India as competing choices.

Answering divisive rhetoric with local roots

The timing is deliberate. The statement says that in light of recent racially charged rhetoric directed at Indian Americans, it is important to emphasise how deeply the community cares about the places it calls home — its neighbourhoods, local nonprofits and universities. Local giving, it argues, does more than fund worthy causes: it builds relationships, trust and camaraderie with neighbours, and helps create stronger, more resilient communities over the long term.

That local emphasis was echoed in the wider summit communiqué. More than 160 leaders from the U.S.-India philanthropy community gathered in Dallas on September 28-29, according to The American Bazaar's coverage of the summit. Their Oct. 2 communiqué, issued to coincide with Gandhi Jayanti, said giving to causes in India, the United States and transnational causes should not be viewed as competing priorities, and condemned attacks based on ethnicity, culture or religion.

What the summit prioritised

Beyond the headline message, speakers in Dallas set out a practical agenda. First, capacity: strengthening nonprofit institutions, including investing in staff training, was presented as essential to lasting impact, rather than relying indefinitely on volunteers. The American Bazaar reported the same theme — that India-focused nonprofits in the U.S. have often underinvested in organisational infrastructure and talent, and that strategic investment in fundraising staff can generate significant returns.

Second, the next generation. Both the GlobeNewswire statement and the summit coverage stress engaging young professionals in philanthropy early, so giving becomes a habit and a skill developed through study and practice, not a late-career afterthought.

Third, preventive health. Speakers directed attention to prevention, particularly efforts to reduce diabetes and cardiovascular disease in India and among Indian Americans. Summit delegates also linked their work to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals and to India's goal of becoming a developed nation by 2047.

Voices from Dallas

The Oct. 14 statement thanked keynote speakers Satish Gupta, president of Gupta Capital Group, and Anurag Jain, managing partner of Perot Jain, and celebrated the philanthropic contributions of the Indian American community in the Greater Dallas area. In the earlier summit sessions reported by The American Bazaar, Jain opened with a keynote on how giving can also benefit the giver, Gupta urged the community at a welcome dinner at the University of Texas at Dallas to contribute to social improvement in both the United States and India and to oppose anti-Indian hate, and local leaders including Raj and Anna Asava of Hunger Mitao were highlighted for Dallas-based work.

Alex Counts, executive director of the India Philanthropy Alliance, closed the September summit by inviting participants to support the fifth India Giving Day on March 12, 2027, and said the alliance would help expand both the quantity and quality of American philanthropy to India while encouraging strategic giving more broadly.

What this means for the diaspora

For Indian American readers, the practical takeaway is twofold. If you already give, the summit's message is to give locally as visibly as you give transnationally — to the school, food bank, hospital and university in your own city — and to consider multi-year support for nonprofit staff and infrastructure, not only programme grants. If you are new to organised giving, India Giving Day on March 12, 2027 is the next concrete entry point the alliance is promoting.

The broader significance is civic. At a moment when rhetoric about immigrants has sharpened, the community's largest philanthropy networks are not retreating into private giving. They are publishing the local record — Dallas neighbourhoods included — and arguing that seva at home is part of what makes the diaspora American.
